At a glance

Best months
  • May and June for seabird colonies and pinewood song
  • September and October for migration on the northern isles
  • October to March for geese

When to Go

Scotland runs on a short, intense summer. The seabird cliffs fill from April and empty by early August, the pinewood specialities are easiest while they are singing in April and May, and the geese arrive in six figures through October. Midsummer daylight in Shetland runs past eleven at night, which is why a June day holds twice the birding a January one does.

Spring

March to June

Seabirds come back to the ledges in March, summer migrants arrive through April, and by May every woodland is singing from before five in the morning.

Go for Breeding seabirds, full song, and the longest days of the year in the north.

Trade off Rooms cost the most from Easter onward, and island boats need booking weeks ahead in June.

Typical daily average
  • March: 3 to 9 °C / 37 to 48 °F
  • April: 4 to 12 °C / 39 to 54 °F
  • May: 7 to 15 °C / 45 to 59 °F
  • June: 10 to 18 °C / 50 to 64 °F

Autumn

July to October

Wader passage builds from July, the coasts fill with migrants through September, and October is when a rarity can turn up almost anywhere.

Go for Big wader counts, seabirds moving past in an onshore wind, and the best chance of a bird from a long way off course.

Trade off Song has stopped, so birds are identified on plumage and call, and the seabird colonies are empty by August.

Typical daily average
  • July: 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F
  • August: 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F
  • September: 10 to 17 °C / 50 to 63 °F
  • October: 8 to 13 °C / 46 to 55 °F

Winter

November to February

Geese, swans and waders pack the estuaries, starlings gather over the reedbeds at dusk, and raptors are easy over open ground.

Go for Six figure goose and wader flocks, murmurations, and reserves you have largely to yourself.

Trade off Daylight is short, especially in Scotland, and island ferries and boat trips run to a thin timetable.

Typical daily average
  • November: 5 to 10 °C / 41 to 50 °F
  • December: 3 to 8 °C / 37 to 46 °F
  • January: 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F
  • February: 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F

An Edinburgh Layover

Edinburgh (EDI), the Firth of Forth, Edinburgh

The Forth reserves are half an hour from the city by train or road. A morning at Musselburgh and Aberlady reaches seaduck, waders and geese and gets you back for an afternoon flight.

The Forth Seabird Weekend

Edinburgh (EDI), North Berwick, Anstruther

Two boats and a shoreline. The Bass Rock from North Berwick, a landing on the Isle of May from either side of the firth, and the estuary reserves in between. Boats need booking well ahead in June and July.

The Solway and Galloway

Glasgow (GLA), Caerlaverock 2 nights, Kirkcudbright and Galloway Forest 1 night, Glasgow (GLA) out

The Solway merse takes the wintering geese and Caerlaverock is where they are watched from. The Galloway forest behind it holds Red Kite, and the Mull of Galloway is the southernmost seabird cliff in Scotland.

Speyside and the Cairngorms

Inverness (INV), Speyside, the Cairngorm plateau

Five days from Inverness reaches every Scottish speciality that lives in pinewood or on high ground. The plateau needs a settled day, so build the week around the forecast rather than the calendar.

The Northern Isles

Aberdeen (ABZ) or Inverness, Orkney, Shetland, Fair Isle

Ten days working north by ferry and light aircraft. Seabird cliffs and long light in June, or migrants and the chance of something extraordinary in late September and October.

Shetland and Orkney

Seabird cliff, moorland and voe on two island groups, reached by an overnight ferry from Aberdeen or a short flight to Sumburgh or Kirkwall

Two island groups at the top of Britain, far enough north that the light barely goes in June. Seabird cliffs are the draw, and both groups sit where a lost migrant makes landfall, so autumn brings birds from three continents.

  • Habitat: Treeless maritime heath and blanket bog on old red sandstone, with sea cliff, geo and voe, and the Loch of Harray and Stenness on Orkney.
  • When: May to July for the seabird cliffs and the phalaropes. September and October on Fair Isle and North Ronaldsay is the drift-migration season the observatories exist for.
  • Getting there: Ferries from Aberdeen to Kirkwall and Lerwick sail overnight, and both islands have airports. Fair Isle and North Ronaldsay are reached by the inter-island plane or the mail boat.
  • Look for: Great Skua, European Storm Petrel, Red-throated Loon, Common Murre, Black Guillemot, Atlantic Puffin
  • Parks and reserves: Hermaness National Nature Reserve, Noss National Nature Reserve, Marwick Head RSPB Reserve, Hoy RSPB Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Sumburgh Head : An RSPB reserve on Shetland's southern tip. The lighthouse visitor centre charges entry and a free clifftop path runs beside it, with puffins within arm's reach.
    • : A clifftop on Shetland's Northmavine peninsula, on foot from a small roadside car park. Fulmars hold every ledge of the volcanic cliffs and skuas pass overhead.
    • Mousa : An uninhabited island with a two thousand year old broch. A booked evening boat runs from Sandsayre, and storm-petrels fly in after dark to nest in the broch walls from late May to mid July.
    • Fair Isle : A small crofting island between Shetland and Orkney, with its own bird observatory and guesthouse. Ferry and light aircraft both serve it, and it is one of Britain's best places for migrants in spring and autumn.
    • Marwick Head : An RSPB clifftop reserve on Orkney Mainland, with a free path past the Kitchener Memorial. Guillemots, kittiwakes and fulmars pack the ledges below.
    • Trumland, Rousay : An RSPB moorland reserve on Rousay, a short ferry from Tingwall. The walk starts at the pier and there are no facilities on site. Hen harriers, merlins and short-eared owls hunt low over the hill.
    • North Ronaldsay : Orkney's most northerly island. Ferry and plane both run from Kirkwall. A bird observatory watches the spring and autumn migrants, and native sheep graze the shore.
    • Old Man of Hoy path, Rackwick : A crofting bay on Hoy where the coast path to the Old Man of Hoy begins. The walk is free from a small car park, great skuas pass overhead and golden eagle is possible.
    • Fetlar : An island on the inter-island ferry network. The hide at Loch of Funzie takes red-necked phalarope in June.
    • Foula : The remotest inhabited island in Britain. It holds one of the largest great skua colonies in the world.
    • RSPB Copinsay : An uninhabited seabird island east of Mainland Orkney. Boats are arranged from Skaill.
    • Stronsay and Sanday : Two low northern isles on the ferry network. Autumn is when the drift migrants arrive.
  • Visitor centres: Sumburgh Head Lighthouse and Visitor Centre, Fair Isle Bird Observatory, North Ronaldsay Bird Observatory
  • Also covers: Eshaness, Fair Isle Bird Observatory, Fetlar, Foula, Hermaness National Nature Reserve, Hoy RSPB Reserve, Kirkwall, Lerwick, Marwick Head RSPB Reserve, Mousa, North Ronaldsay Bird Observatory, Noss National Nature Reserve, Old Man of Hoy path, Rackwick, RSPB Copinsay, Stromness, Stronsay and Sanday, Sumburgh Head Lighthouse and Visitor Centre, Trumland, Rousay, Unst, Westray
  • Also watch for: Grey and harbour seals haul out on skerries and beaches all year, with grey seal pups born on quiet shores from October to December. Shetland holds Britain's densest population of otters, most active around dawn and dusk on the tideline, and orca pass along the coast most often between April and August.

The Outer Hebrides

Machair, moorland and sea loch strung across a low green archipelago, reached by ferry from Ullapool, Uig or Oban, or a short flight to Stornoway or Benbecula

A hundred miles of Hebridean island chain with shell sand beaches on the west side and peat moor behind. The machair is still farmed in a way that suits corncrakes, and both eagles are easier here than almost anywhere in Britain.

  • Habitat: Machair grassland on shell sand along the west coast, backed by blanket bog and lochan on the Lewisian gneiss.
  • When: May to July for corncrake in the machair and breeding waders at densities found nowhere else in Britain. Winter holds the barnacle and white-fronted geese.
  • Getting there: Ferries from Ullapool to Stornoway, Uig to Tarbert and Lochboisdale, and Oban to Barra. A car is needed, and the causeways link the Uists end to end.
  • Look for: Corn Crake, Golden Eagle, White-tailed Eagle, Red-throated Loon, Red-necked Phalarope, Corn Bunting
  • Parks and reserves: Balranald Nature Reserve, Loch na Muilne Nature Reserve, St Kilda National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Balranald : An RSPB reserve on North Uist's machair coast, the shell-sand grassland behind Atlantic dunes. A visitor caravan is staffed in summer and access is free all year. Corncrakes call from the iris beds, and dunlin and redshank breed on the machair.
    • : A headland at the north end of the Balranald reserve, walked from the same car park. It is the best seabird watchpoint in the islands in a westerly blow, for skuas and the chance of Leach's Storm-Petrel.
    • Loch na Muilne : An RSPB reserve on Lewis, a level walk from a small car park at Arnol. Red-necked phalaropes spin on the loch in summer among breeding waders.
    • : A working lighthouse at the northern tip of Lewis, with free clifftop access. Gannets and skuas pass close inshore in a northerly wind and a sea eagle sometimes crosses.
    • : Britain's highest sea cliffs, crossed to by day boat or charter yacht from Leverburgh, Miavaig or Berneray. The largest seabird colony in the northeast Atlantic holds gannets, puffins and storm-petrels.
  • Visitor centres:
    • North Harris Eagle Observatory, A timber hide built by the North Harris Trust, about half an hour up Glen Meavaig from a roadside car park. Entry is free and it looks along the territory of a resident pair of golden eagles.
  • Also covers: Aird an Rùnair, Balivanich, Balranald Nature Reserve, Butt of Lewis, Castlebay, Loch na Muilne Nature Reserve, Lochboisdale, Lochmaddy, North Harris Eagle Observatory, St Kilda National Nature Reserve, Stornoway
  • Also watch for: Otters fish the sea lochs and machair coast at dawn and dusk throughout the year, and grey seals haul out on skerries with pups appearing from October. Minke whales and basking sharks pass offshore between June and September, best looked for from a headland such as Aird an Rùnair when the wind blows onshore.

The Northwest Highlands and Sutherland

Peatland, sea cliffs and mountain across the far northwest of Sutherland and Wester Ross

Bare quartzite hills, blanket bog and sea cliff along the emptiest coast in Britain. Distances are long and the roads are single track, so this is a region to give days to rather than hours.

  • Habitat: Sandstone and quartzite hills over the Assynt lochan country, with Caledonian pine remnants and the Cromarty and Dornoch firths to the east.
  • When: April to July for divers on the hill lochs and the breeding raptors. October to March fills the firths with wildfowl and waders.
  • Getting there: The A835 and A837 run in from Inverness, two to three hours to Ullapool and Lochinver. The North Coast 500 covers the same ground and fills the road in summer.
  • Look for: Golden Eagle, Black-throated Loon, Red-throated Loon, Common Greenshank, Great Skua, Atlantic Puffin
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Handa Island (island reserve), A Scottish Wildlife Trust reserve, on an on-demand ferry from Tarbet in summer, entry by donation. Common murres, razorbills, Atlantic puffins and great skuas hold the cliffs.
    • RSPB Forsinard Flows (RSPB reserve)
    • Loch Fleet National Nature Reserve
    • Beinn Eighe and Loch Maree Islands National Nature Reserve
    • Knockan Crag National Nature Reserve, A NatureScot reserve with a car park and a geology trail through folded rock, free to enter. The views run wide across Assynt, ravens are constant and golden eagle is possible.
  • Stops:
    • Flows Boardwalk and Viewing Tower, Forsinard : An RSPB boardwalk trail and viewing tower over blanket bog, free from the visitor centre. Golden plovers, dunlin, hen harriers and divers use the peatland pools.
    • Littleferry, Loch Fleet : A beach car park and dune path at the mouth of Loch Fleet National Nature Reserve, free at any time. Ospreys fish the estuary and seals haul out on the sandbanks.
    • : A sandy bay by the car park at Balnakeil, free at any time. Red-throated loons and long-tailed ducks winter offshore and snow buntings work the machair.
    • : A clifftop and dune walk north from Balnakeil across access land, open on days when the firing range is clear. Atlantic puffins and great skuas sit below the headland.
    • : A roadside pull-in by a ruined castle on Loch Assynt, free at any time. Golden eagles cross the hills and black-throated loons hold the loch in summer.
    • Aultroy Visitor Centre and Woodland Trail, Beinn Eighe : A NatureScot visitor centre with waymarked trails through pinewood and up onto the mountain, free to enter. Golden eagles cross the ridge, and pine martens and crossbills use the woods.
    • RSPB Udale Bay : A hide over the Cromarty Firth on the Black Isle. A rising tide is when wigeon, godwit and redshank come close.
    • RSPB Nigg Bay : The other side of the Cromarty Firth. A hide and a bund run out into the mudflats.
    • Inverpolly and Ben Mor Coigach : Sandstone hills and lochan country north of Ullapool. The walking starts from the Achiltibuie road.
    • Clo Mor cliffs : The highest sea cliffs on the British mainland, east of Cape Wrath. A ferry and minibus from Durness reach them.
    • The Isle of Skye : An island reached by bridge at Kyle. Sea eagle crosses the sea lochs, with the Cuillin and Trotternish ridges above them.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Forsinard Flows Visitor Centre, Aultroy Visitor Centre, Beinn Eighe
  • Also covers: Ardvreck Castle, Loch Assynt, Aultroy Visitor Centre and Woodland Trail, Beinn Eighe, Aultroy Visitor Centre, Beinn Eighe, Balnakeil Bay, Beinn Eighe and Loch Maree Islands National Nature Reserve, Clo Mor cliffs, Durness, Faraid Head, Flows Boardwalk and Viewing Tower, Forsinard, Handa Island, Inverpolly and Ben Mor Coigach, Kinlochewe, Knockan Crag National Nature Reserve, Lairg, Littleferry, Loch Fleet, Loch Fleet National Nature Reserve, Portree, RSPB Forsinard Flows Visitor Centre, RSPB Nigg Bay, RSPB Udale Bay, Scourie, The Isle of Skye, Ullapool
  • Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on Handa's rocks throughout the year, and minke whales, dolphins and the occasional basking shark pass offshore in summer. Pine martens and wildcats move through Beinn Eighe's ancient pinewoods, best looked for around dawn and dusk.

The Highlands and Speyside

Ancient pinewood, high plateau and strath along the upper Spey, about an hour's drive south of Inverness

Old Caledonian pinewood runs along the strath with high plateau above it, and it holds a handful of birds that live nowhere else in Britain. Almost everything worth seeing sits within forty minutes of Aviemore.

  • Habitat: Caledonian pine forest on the Spey floodplain rising to arctic-alpine plateau on the Cairngorms, with lochs and moorland between.
  • When: April to June is the season: capercaillie leks, crested tit and Scottish crossbill in the pines, and dotterel and ptarmigan on the plateau once the snow clears.
  • Getting there: The A9 reaches Aviemore in two and a half hours from Edinburgh, and the Highland Main Line stops there. Loch Garten and Abernethy are signed from Boat of Garten.
  • Look for: Western Capercaillie, Scottish Crossbill, Crested Tit, Rock Ptarmigan, Osprey, Golden Eagle, Black Grouse, Eurasian Dotterel
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Cairngorms National Park
    • Abernethy National Nature Reserve
    • Loch Ruthven RSPB Reserve
    • Insh Marshes RSPB Reserve
    • Craigellachie National Nature Reserve, A birch woodland reserve on the edge of Aviemore, on foot through a subway under the A9. Access is free and peregrine falcons cross the crags above the trees.
  • Stops:
    • Abernethy Forest : Old Caledonian pinewood, open all year with no entry fee. Waymarked paths circle Loch Garten and Loch Mallachie, and crested tit and Scottish crossbill move through the pines.
    • Loch an Eilein, Rothiemurchus : A private estate path circling a loch with a ruined castle island, free to walk. Crested tits and Scottish crossbills hold the pines and ospreys sometimes fish the water.
    • Loch Ruthven : An RSPB reserve with a single hide, a short walk from the car park and free to visit. It is the UK's most important breeding site for Slavonian Grebe.
    • Insh Marshes : An RSPB floodplain reserve on the River Spey with two waymarked trails and hides, free to visit. Curlew and redshank breed in summer and whooper swans winter on the marsh.
    • Cairn Gorm plateau : A high open plateau. The funicular to Ptarmigan station reaches it, or the walk up from the Coire Cas car park. Ptarmigan, dotterel and snow bunting hold territory here in summer.
    • Findhorn Valley : A single-track road up a glacial glen. The car park at the head is the watchpoint for golden eagle and other raptors over the ridges.
    • Lochindorb : A moorland loch on an unfenced road. Red-throated diver holds the water and the moor around it is visible from the car.
  • Visitor centres:
    • Loch Garten Osprey Centre, An RSPB reserve with a seasonal visitor centre and a live nest camera. Entry is charged from April to August and a free pinewood path runs alongside. Ospreys fish the loch and crested tits come to the feeders.
    • Cairngorm Mountain
  • Also covers: Abernethy Forest, Abernethy National Nature Reserve, Aviemore, Boat of Garten, Cairn Gorm plateau, Cairngorm Mountain, Cairngorms National Park, Craigellachie National Nature Reserve, Findhorn Valley, Insh Marshes RSPB Reserve, Inverness, Loch an Eilein, Rothiemurchus, Loch Garten Osprey Centre, Loch Ruthven RSPB Reserve, Lochindorb, Nethy Bridge
  • Also watch for: Red squirrels are active year round in the pinewoods, and pine martens, mostly active after dark, are sometimes watched from hides at dusk in summer. Mountain hares turn white for winter on the high ground from November to March, and a herd of reindeer grazes freely on the hills above Glenmore.

Argyll, Mull and Islay

Sea lochs, machair and raised bog across the southern Hebrides, three hours from Glasgow plus a ferry crossing

Sea lochs, oak woods and raised bog sit behind short ferries from a coast within an easy drive of Glasgow. Mull is where people come for eagles, Islay for wintering geese, and both hold chough.

  • Habitat: Sea loch and basalt island, with Atlantic oakwood on the mainland and machair and improved grassland on Islay.
  • When: October to April for the Islay barnacle and Greenland white-fronted geese, which is most of their world population. May to August for eagles and the Mull sea lochs.
  • Getting there: Ferries from Oban to Mull and Kennacraig to Islay, both bookable and both busy in summer. Islay also has an airport with flights from Glasgow.
  • Look for: White-tailed Eagle, Golden Eagle, Atlantic Puffin, Barnacle Goose, Red-billed Chough, Black Grouse
  • Parks and reserves: RSPB Loch Gruinart Nature Reserve (RSPB reserve), RSPB The Oa (RSPB reserve), Taynish National Nature Reserve, Glasdrum Wood National Nature Reserve, Staffa National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • : A free community hide beside the ferry slipway on the Sound of Mull, always open and run by Forestry and Land Scotland. White-tailed eagles and otters work the open water.
    • : A small ferry slipway where boats leave for Ulva and wildlife trips run to Staffa and the Treshnish Isles, open to any passer-by. Otters work the tideline and eagles pass overhead.
    • : The ferry village at the tip of the Ross of Mull, where boats leave for Iona and for puffin trips to the Treshnish Isles. Black guillemots nest around the harbour.
    • : A boat trip landing on the largest of the Treshnish Isles, weather dependent and booked through operators from Mull or Iona. Puffins nest in burrows close enough to touch.
    • : Farmland and dune pasture on the Rinns of Islay, on public road. Around a tenth of Britain's breeding chough forage on the short turf.
    • : A broad sea loch on Islay. Roadside pull-ins between Bridgend and Port Charlotte give the views. Divers and scoters raft on the water through winter.
    • RSPB Loch Gruinart hide trail : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and free hides over the tidal flats, open to all. Barnacle and white-fronted geese graze here in their thousands each winter.
    • Staffa : A boat trip landing on a National Nature Reserve, run from Fionnphort, Iona or Ulva Ferry between April and September. Puffins nest on the clifftop above Fingal's Cave.
    • Ardnamurchan : The westernmost peninsula on the British mainland, on the Corran ferry. Sea eagle and otter both occur, and a long single-track road runs out to the point.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Loch Gruinart Visitor Centre, Mull Eagle Watch (Forestry and Land Scotland)
  • Also covers: Ardnamurchan, Bowmore, Craignure, Fionnphort, Fishnish Community Wildlife Hide, Glasdrum Wood National Nature Reserve, Kilchoman, Loch Indaal, Lunga, Treshnish Isles, Mull Eagle Watch (Forestry and Land Scotland), Oban, Port Charlotte, RSPB Loch Gruinart hide trail, RSPB Loch Gruinart Nature Reserve, RSPB Loch Gruinart Visitor Centre, RSPB The Oa, Staffa National Nature Reserve, Taynish National Nature Reserve, Tobermory, Ulva Ferry
  • Also watch for: Minke whales and basking sharks pass close along the Hebridean coast between May and August, and otters work the sea lochs and shorelines around Mull and Islay year round. Red deer gather on the moors of Mull and mainland Argyll for the rut in September and October.

The Firth of Forth, Fife and the Borders coast

Basalt and sandstone seabird islands across the Firth of Forth, half an hour from Edinburgh by road or boat

The Bass Rock carries the largest northern gannet colony in the world, and the Isle of May lets you walk among puffins between boats. Both sail from North Berwick, and the coast either side takes waders and sea duck through the winter.

  • Habitat: Volcanic plugs and basalt islands in a firth, with sandstone cliff at St Abb's and estuarine mud and ash lagoons on the inner shore.
  • When: April to August for the Bass Rock gannets and the Isle of May puffins, which is when the boats run. Winter brings sea duck and waders to the inner firth.
  • Getting there: North Berwick is half an hour from Edinburgh by train and the boats leave from the harbour. St Abb's Head is signed off the A1 at Coldingham.
  • Look for: Northern Gannet, Atlantic Puffin, Common Murre, Black-legged Kittiwake, Pink-footed Goose, Horned Grebe
  • Parks and reserves: Isle of May National Nature Reserve, Aberlady Bay Local Nature Reserve, St Abb's Head National Nature Reserve, Tentsmuir National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Bass Rock boat trip : A boat trip from North Berwick harbour that circles the rock, run by the Scottish Seabird Centre. The world's largest gannet colony packs more than 150,000 birds onto the stack.
    • : A National Nature Reserve, by boat from North Berwick or Anstruther. The landing gives a few hours to walk freely or join a guide, among puffins, guillemots and grey seals.
    • St Abb's Head clifftop path : A National Trust for Scotland nature reserve with a free clifftop path, open at any time. Guillemots, razorbills and kittiwakes nest on the ledges from May to July.
    • : Scotland's first Local Nature Reserve, crossed by a wooden footbridge over the estuary, free and open at any time. Pink-footed geese roost here in their thousands each autumn.
    • : Gravel scrapes and hides on former ash lagoons beside the coast path at Musselburgh, free to walk. Waders, terns and seaduck gather close to the hides.
    • Tentsmuir Point : A National Nature Reserve of dune, forest and shifting sandbanks on the Fife coast, open at any time. Pink-footed geese arrive in autumn and grey seals haul out on the point.
    • Fife Ness and Kilminning Coast : A clifftop headland and wildlife reserve at the tip of the Fife peninsula, free to walk with no set hours. It is a classic seabird watchpoint for skuas and divers passing offshore.
  • Visitor centres: Scottish Seabird Centre, North Berwick
  • Also covers: Aberlady Bay boardwalk, Aberlady Bay Local Nature Reserve, Anstruther, Bass Rock boat trip, Eyemouth, Fife Ness and Kilminning Coast, Isle of May landing trip, Isle of May National Nature Reserve, Levenhall Links, Musselburgh, Scottish Seabird Centre, North Berwick, St Abb's Head clifftop path, St Abb's Head National Nature Reserve, Tentsmuir National Nature Reserve, Tentsmuir Point
  • Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the rocks around the Isle of May and St Abb's Head, with pups born on the Isle of May between October and December. Harbour porpoises and, less often, minke whales and bottlenose dolphins turn up on the seabird boat trips through summer.

Aberdeenshire, Moray and the Northeast coast

Scotland's only mainland gannetry, the largest eider colony in Britain and a goose roost counted in tens of thousands, along one coast

Troup Head is the one place on the Scottish mainland where gannets nest, and the cliff is walked to rather than sailed to. The geese arrive at Strathbeg from Iceland and Svalbard in October and stay until spring, and the eiders gather off the Ythan dunes where the terns breed. The Moray Firth beyond takes the sea duck.

  • Habitat: Sandstone and conglomerate sea cliff, dune and estuary, with the Loch of Strathbeg dune loch behind its bar.
  • When: October to March for the geese at Strathbeg and the Moray Firth sea duck. April to July for the Troup Head gannets and the Ythan eiders and terns.
  • Getting there: The A90 runs north from Aberdeen to Peterhead and Fraserburgh, and the A98 turns west along the Moray coast. Troup Head is signed from Gardenstown and the last stretch is a farm track.
  • Look for: Northern Gannet, Common Eider, Pink-footed Goose, Velvet Scoter, Long-tailed Duck, Black-legged Kittiwake
  • National parks:
    • RSPB Loch of Strathbeg, The largest dune loch in Britain, with hides over the water. Pink-footed and barnacle geese roost here through the winter.
    • RSPB Fowlsheugh, Three kilometres of sandstone cliff south of Stonehaven. Guillemot, razorbill, kittiwake and puffin hold it from April into July.
    • RSPB Troup Head, The only mainland gannet colony in Scotland. A clifftop path from the car park reaches it, so no boat is involved.
    • Sands of Forvie National Nature Reserve
    • St Cyrus National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Ythan Estuary and the Sands of Forvie : The largest eider colony in Britain, with terns on the dunes behind. The estuary is walked from Newburgh.
    • Girdle Ness : A headland inside Aberdeen city, with the sea on three sides and a lighthouse path. An easterly wind is what brings the migrants in.
    • St Cyrus : A National Nature Reserve of dune and cliff at the mouth of the Esk. The visitor centre sits on the beach road.
    • Findhorn Bay : A tidal basin behind Culbin Forest that takes waders and geese. The bar at Findhorn village holds the sea duck.
    • Spey Bay : Shingle at the mouth of the Spey. The Moray Firth sea duck gather here and the dolphins come inshore.
    • Burghead and Lossiemouth : Two harbours on the southern Moray Firth. Long-tailed duck, velvet scoter and divers hold them through the winter.
  • Visitor centres: Scottish Dolphin Centre, Spey Bay
  • Also covers: Banff, Burghead and Lossiemouth, Findhorn Bay, Fraserburgh, Girdle Ness, Peterhead, RSPB Fowlsheugh, RSPB Loch of Strathbeg, RSPB Troup Head, Sands of Forvie National Nature Reserve, Scottish Dolphin Centre, Spey Bay, St Cyrus National Nature Reserve, Stonehaven, Ythan Estuary and the Sands of Forvie
  • Also watch for: Bottlenose dolphins hold the Moray Firth and show from the shore at Spey Bay and Chanonry. Grey seals haul out on the Ythan sands.

The Solway and Galloway

Merse, forest and firth on the Solway coast, ninety minutes from Carlisle

A shallow firth with merse and mudflat on its northern shore, forest and loch behind. The whole Svalbard barnacle goose population winters here, which is a spectacle few places in Europe can match.

  • Habitat: Merse saltmarsh and intertidal sand on the firth, with raised bog, Galloway forest and the granite hills behind.
  • When: October to March. The entire Svalbard barnacle goose population winters on the Solway, and the merse holds pink-footed geese and whooper swans with them.
  • Getting there: The A75 and A710 run the Solway shore from Dumfries. Caerlaverock is twenty minutes from the town and Mersehead is signed off the A710.
  • Look for: Barnacle Goose, Pink-footed Goose, Hen Harrier, Red Kite, Osprey, Eurasian Curlew, Black Grouse
  • Parks and reserves: Galloway Forest Park (reserve), Caerlaverock National Nature Reserve, Wigtown Bay Local Nature Reserve, Mull of Galloway National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Mersehead : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre, hides and two waymarked trails, free to members and by donation otherwise. Barnacle geese and starling murmurations fill the winter, and natterjack toads call in spring.
    • RSPB Ken-Dee Marshes : An RSPB reserve on Loch Ken with one hide by a small car park, free to enter. Whooper swans and goldeneye winter here and ospreys fish in summer.
    • : A harbour car park giving free roadside views over Wigtown Bay Local Nature Reserve at any time. Pink-footed geese and hen harriers work the merse in winter.
    • Mull of Galloway : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and a clifftop path around Scotland's most southerly point, free to walk with paid parking. Gannets, guillemots and peregrines hold the cliffs.
    • Clatteringshaws Loch, Galloway Forest Park : A loch-side car park and forest drive within Galloway Forest Park, free at any time. Red kites cross the forest and ospreys fish the loch in summer.
    • Glentrool, Galloway Forest Park : A Forestry and Land Scotland visitor centre with waymarked trails through oakwood and conifer plantation, free to enter. Goshawks display in early spring, and crossbills and siskins hold the conifers.
    • : A roadside viewpoint by the lighthouse on the Solway coast, free at any time. Red-throated loons and common goldeneye winter offshore and waders work the falling tide.
    • WWT Caerlaverock : A WWT reserve with a visitor centre and an entry fee, by road south of Dumfries. Thousands of barnacle geese from Svalbard graze the merse each winter.
  • Visitor centres:
    • WWT Caerlaverock Wetland Centre, A WWT wetland centre with hides, a visitor centre and an entry fee, ten minutes from Dumfries. Barnacle geese and whooper swans come close to the hides in winter.
    • RSPB Mersehead Visitor Centre
    • Glentrool and Kirroughtree Visitor Centres, Galloway Forest Park
  • Also covers: Caerlaverock National Nature Reserve, Clatteringshaws Loch, Galloway Forest Park, Dumfries, Glentrool and Kirroughtree Visitor Centres, Galloway Forest Park, Glentrool, Galloway Forest Park, Kirkcudbright, Mull of Galloway National Nature Reserve, Newton Stewart, RSPB Ken-Dee Marshes, RSPB Mersehead Visitor Centre, Southerness Point, Stranraer, Wigtown Bay Local Nature Reserve, Wigtown Harbour and the Merse, WWT Caerlaverock Wetland Centre
  • Also watch for: Natterjack toads spawn in the dune slacks at Mersehead between April and June, one of Scotland's few sites for Britain's rarest amphibian. Red deer roar through the rut in Galloway Forest Park each October, and the forest's wild goats graze the open hill above Clatteringshaws all year round.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Scotland?

May and June for seabird colonies, pinewood song and the longest days. September and October for migrants on the northern isles. October to March for geese in six figures on the Solway and Islay.

Do I need a car?

For most of Scotland, yes. Aviemore is the exception worth knowing: the train reaches it and Speyside's best ground is within a bike ride. The Forth reserves work from Edinburgh by train, and the west coast ferry ports are all on the rail network.

How many places to stay are above?

340, every one of them carrying a Green Tourism award confirmed in the scheme's own register on the date shown on its chip. That is a much smaller number than the accommodation available near these reserves, and it is deliberate: a certification you cannot check is a claim rather than evidence.

Do I need to book the island boats in advance?

Yes, and earlier than feels necessary. Isle of May landings, the Handa ferry and the Bass Rock trips are all weather dependent and all sell out in June and July, so build a spare day into any trip that depends on landing somewhere.

What about the midges?

Highland midges are out from late May to early September, worst on still damp evenings in the west, and they change how you plan a dusk watch. A head net is light and worth carrying from June onward.

How long are the days?

Midsummer in Shetland gives light past eleven at night and a dawn chorus that starts around three, so a June day holds two or three sessions. Midwinter in the same place gives around six hours, which changes how many sites fit into a day.

Where do the rarities turn up?

On the northern isles. Fair Isle, North Ronaldsay and Shetland all sit where a bird blown off course makes its first landfall, and each has an observatory or a warden logging what arrives. October is the month and an easterly airflow is the condition.

Can I get to the high tops safely?

The Cairngorm plateau is serious ground with fast weather, and ptarmigan and dotterel live on it. The funicular reaches the Ptarmigan station, and from there a short walk in settled conditions reaches the habitat without a mountain day.

Is Scottish birding good for a beginner?

It is one of the easiest places to start. The reserves have hides, paths and staff, the list is small enough to learn, and a seabird colony gives close views of a dozen species in an afternoon without any skill in finding them.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, Scotland has 17 local bird clubs across 17 regions. See every Scottish club by region.

RSPB Scotland BirdLife in the UK, and the owner of many of the reserves above. Membership pays for itself quickly if you plan to visit more than a handful. Visit Scottish Ornithologists' Club The club for Scotland, with local branches, a library at Aberlady and the annual Scottish Bird Report. Visit NatureScot The nature agency, which runs the national nature reserves and publishes the access and species information behind them. Visit BTO Scotland The volunteer survey and ringing body behind almost every Scottish population figure, with local groups by region. Visit Scottish Wildlife Trust Runs Handa and many smaller reserves, and organises walks that visitors are welcome to join. Visit
